overview: This two-page Department of State list of papers inventories three items filed under “Public Press - Japan”: a 1940 despatch enclosing Japan Times cartoons about the United States, a 1941 telegram concerning a newspaper rumor that the United States sought four naval bases in China as part of a peace arrangement, and a further 1941 report on the increasingly truculent and aggressive tone of the Japanese press toward the United States. The underlying despatches, telegrams, letters, and clippings are not present in the supplied text; the list instead provides dates, brief descriptions, and cross-references to related decimal files.

subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Public Press—Japan
subfiles.about: A two-page archival list describes three Grew communications concerning Japanese press treatment of the United States in 1940–1941.
subfiles.summary: The first entry records an August 5, 1940 communication enclosing three Japan Times cartoons devoted to the United States, published on July 19, July 30, and August 2. The second, continued onto page 2, concerns a November 6, 1941 telegram seeking the text of an embassy letter published in the Japan Times and Advertiser about a rumor that the United States wanted to maintain and use four naval bases in China in return for a peace arrangement; it cross-references file 893.24/1193. The third entry, dated November 7 and apparently also from 1941, describes the truculent and aggressive substance and tone of the Japanese press toward the United States and notes an authorized informal comment made in a meeting with the Foreign Minister; it cross-references file 711.94/2422.

interest: The list is useful as a finding aid for reconstructing State Department monitoring of Japanese newspapers immediately before the Pacific War. Its three entries juxtapose visual satire, a strategically significant rumor about American naval bases in China, and an embassy assessment of increasingly hostile press rhetoric. The cited decimal-file references may allow historians to locate related documents even though the underlying communications and clippings are absent from this surviving file extract.
